statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips used on dissolved drug and read by trained staff, compared with laboratory analysis (GC/MS) of the same samples or with the known content of prepared solutions, the strips showed fentanyl in almost every sample that contained it, down to very low concentrations, but the lowest concentration they detected differed widely between studies, brands and production lots. In 106 police-seized samples that earlier GC/MS had found to contain fentanyl (two US forensic laboratories, 2017), one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 104 (52 of 52 in one laboratory, 52 of 54 in the other; 98 in 100, editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%); both samples it missed contained fentanyl alone (Green et al., 2020). Drug-checking data from British Columbia, known only second-hand, point the same way: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples missed, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less (McCrae et al., 2020, as cited by Halifax et al., 2024); a scoping review relays sensitivity of about 96 to 98 in 100 from that study and one validation study (Kutscher et al., 2024). In pure fentanyl solutions, the lowest concentration detected was 100 to 150 ng/mL (Green et al.); 25 ng/mL by eye with five strips per concentration (Lockwood et al., 2021); a positive reading at 100 ng/mL on all four brands tested, though two showed only a barely visible test band there, which the makers' rule (any visible band means negative) would read as negative (Bergh et al., 2021, single readings); 20 ng/mL for two lots obtained in 2017 against 200 ng/mL for three lots obtained in 2021 (Halifax et al., 2024, duplicate strips); and 500 ng/mL for strips whose listed cut-off was 200 ng/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b), a 25-fold range overall (editors' calculation). The forensic GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip (3.1 and 100 µg/mL), the seized samples were selected on known content and tested as powders by chemists blind to it, nearly all data come from one brand, and none of these studies measured how people prepare and read strips at home. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In laboratory tests, fentanyl test strips showed fentanyl in almost all drug samples that contained it: 104 of 106 police-seized samples in one study. They can pick up very small amounts, but the smallest amount they found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches of strips. Trained staff did these tests, mostly with one brand; how well strips work when people test at home was not measured.
population: Drug samples in laboratories: 210 police-seized samples from two US cities (2017), drug-checking samples in British Columbia (second-hand) and fentanyl reference standards dissolved in water or ethanol
exposure: Urine fentanyl immunoassay test strips used off-label on dissolved drug (mostly BTNX Rapid Response; four brands in one study), read by trained laboratory staff
comparator: Earlier forensic GC/MS analysis of the same samples, or the known concentration of prepared solutions
outcome: Whether the strip showed fentanyl when it was present (sensitivity), and the lowest fentanyl concentration it detected
magnitude: Seized samples (Green et al., 2020): sensitivity 100.0% (52/52) and 96.3% (52/54) at the two laboratories; 104/106 = 98.1% pooled (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%, editors' calculation). Lowest concentration detected in pure fentanyl solutions: 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL, that is 100–150 ng/mL (Green et al.); 25 ng/mL by eye (Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on four brands, two with a barely visible band only (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL for 2021 lots (Halifax et al., 2024); 500 ng/mL, listed cut-off 200 ng/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Second-hand: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive drug-checking samples missed (McCrae et al., 2020, via Halifax et al.); sensitivity about 96.3–98% (via Kutscher et al., 2024).

evidence.locator: Results › Sensitivity and specificity, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Against earlier forensic GC/MS, the BTNX fentanyl strip read positive in all 52 fentanyl-positive Baltimore samples (sensitivity 100.0%) and in 52 of 54 Providence samples (96.3%); the two samples it missed contained fentanyl only. Fentanyl-positive samples held fentanyl alone (29 and 35) or with heroin, cocaine, acetyl or furanyl fentanyl or 4-ANPP (Table 2). Editors' calculation: 104 of 106 overall, 98.1% (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%).

evidence.locator: Methods › Limits of detection procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Results › Limit of detection, 1st paragraph; Table 1 and footnotes (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: Fentanyl reference standards in ethanol, tested in triplicate at falling concentrations: the strip's limit of detection was 0.150 mcg/mL in Baltimore and 0.100 mcg/mL in Providence, the lowest of all methods tested, including the forensic GC/MS (100 mcg/mL in Baltimore, 3.1 mcg/mL in Providence); Raman 25 mcg/mL, 250 times higher than the strip; FTIR 3–4% by weight. Editors' conversion: 150 and 100 ng/mL.

evidence.locator: Methods › Devices tested, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Methods › Sensitivity and specificity procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Samples were 210 powders and pills seized by two police departments in cases of personal quantities (exhibits of 1 g or less, or fewer than 50 bags), selected from laboratory records as 106 fentanyl-positive and 104 fentanyl-negative by earlier GC/MS, and tested in September and October 2017 by chemists blind to their content; strip samples were dissolved in tap water (Baltimore) or deionized water (Providence) after a 30-minute strip training. The strip is approved in Canada, not the US, for urine and was used off-label; it shows presence only. The amount of sample dissolved and the strip lot are not reported (study card).

evidence.locator: Methods › Fentanyl test strips; Preparation of drug solutions (p. 2); Table 1, fentanyl row (p. 2); Results › Interpretation of test results, 1st paragraph (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Four urine strip brands (Rapid Response, Rapid Self Test and One Step, cut-off 20 ng/mL; Nal van Minden, 10 ng/mL) were dipped in fentanyl dissolved in Type 1 water. All four read positive at 100 and 1000 ng/mL, but at 100 ng/mL two brands (Rapid Response, Rapid Self Test) showed a barely visible test band, graded + by the authors, while the makers' instructions call a test negative whenever two bands appear, however faint. Between 10 and 250 ng/mL the results were highly concentration dependent, so the authors graded bands on four levels and counted no band or a barely visible band as positive. No replicates are reported.

evidence.extracted: Fentanyl spiked into water at nine concentrations from 10 µg/mL down to 10 ng/mL and tested in duplicate on each of five lots of BTNX Rapid Response strips (20 ng/mL urine cut-off), read by two people and recorded by consensus: the two lots obtained and tested in 2017 read positive down to 20 ng/mL, the three lots obtained in 2021 and tested in summer 2022 only down to 200 ng/mL, ten times higher.

evidence.extracted: A Cerilliant fentanyl standard, evaporated from methanol and diluted in deionized water, was tested with five strips at each of 125, 100, 83, 63, 50, 25 and 5 ng/mL (BTNX Rapid Response, lots D808009 and DOA903194): the limit judged by eye was 25 ng/mL. evidence.extracted: The scoping review relays, without appraising the studies, sensitivity of about 96.3–98% and specificity of 89.2–89.4% for fentanyl when strips are used for direct drug testing (its references 16 and 17). Editors' note: these are Park et al. (2022), a validation study sharing authors (Park, Sherman, Clarke) with Green et al. (2020), and McCrae et al. (2020), the British Columbia drug-checking data cited by Halifax et al.; the lower end of the range, 96.3%, equals Green et al.'s Providence figure; neither study was read, so neither is counted as an independent estimate.

risk_of_bias.note: Every laboratory study is at high risk of bias by QUADAS-2 (study cards): Green et al. selected samples on known GC/MS status (106 with and 104 without fentanyl) and used a reference less sensitive than the strip; Bergh et al. graded bands after seeing them, with readers not described as blind; Halifax et al. tested old and new lots in different rounds; Lockwood et al.'s limit rests on a reading rule its own text contradicts. These problems bear most on specificity and borderline readings; counted once.

inconsistency.note: Sensitivity on real samples comes from one study (Green et al.) and agrees with second-hand drug-checking data (4 of 173 missed). Detection limits span 25-fold (20 to 500 ng/mL); the claim states the range, and part of it follows lot, brand and reading rule (Halifax et al.; Bergh et al.), so it is not rated down again.

indirectness.note: Trained laboratory staff, pure fentanyl in water or seized samples tested as powders, mostly one brand; people ask how strips work on their own drugs at home.

imprecision.note: 104 of 106 (95% CI 93.4–99.5%); detection limits from replicated strips in most studies (triplicates, Green et al.; five strips per level, Lockwood et al.; duplicates on five lots, Halifax et al.); single readings only in Bergh et al.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence that compares the strip with a reference method starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded: laboratory detection of fentanyl, not home use and not effects on behaviour or overdose, which are separate questions. Status replicated: independent teams in five laboratories (Green et al.; Lockwood et al.; Bergh et al.; Halifax et al.; Sisco et al., 2024b) detected fentanyl at ng/mL concentrations; only Green et al. measured sensitivity on seized samples. Overlap: the review's sensitivity range comes from a study sharing authors with Green et al. and from the drug-checking data cited by Halifax et al., so it is not counted separately. Sisco et al. (2024b) is filed in-vitro and adds one detection limit.
